### GitHub Vulnerability Alerts

#### [CVE-2025-68429](https://redirect.github.com/storybookjs/storybook/security/advisories/GHSA-8452-54wp-rmv6)

On December 11th, the Storybook team received a responsible disclosure alerting them to a potential vulnerability in certain built and published Storybooks. 

The vulnerability is a bug in how Storybook handles environment variables defined in a `.env` file, which could, in specific circumstances, lead to those variables being unexpectedly bundled into the artifacts created by the `storybook build` command. When a built Storybook is published to the web, the bundle’s source is viewable, thus potentially exposing those variables to anyone with access. If those variables contained secrets, they should be considered compromised.

## Who is impacted?

For a project to be vulnerable to this issue, it must:

- Build the Storybook (i.e. run `storybook build` directly or indirectly) in a directory that contains a `.env` file (including variants like `.env.local`)
- The `.env` file contains sensitive secrets
- Use Storybook version `7.0.0` or above
- Publish the built Storybook to the web

Storybooks built without a `.env` file at build time are not affected, including common CI-based builds where secrets are provided via platform environment variables rather than `.env` files. [description truncated to fit budget]

### GitHub Vulnerability Alerts

#### [CVE-2025-64764](https://redirect.github.com/withastro/astro/security/advisories/GHSA-wrwg-2hg8-v723)

## Summary
After some research it appears that it is possible to obtain a reflected XSS when the server islands feature is used in the targeted application, **regardless of what was intended by the component template(s)**.

## Details
Server islands run in their own isolated context outside of the page request and use the following pattern path to hydrate the page: `/_server-islands/[name]`. These paths can be called via GET or POST and use three parameters:

- `e`: component to export
- `p`: the transmitted properties, encrypted
- `s`: for the slots

Slots are placeholders for external HTML content, and therefore allow, by default, the injection of code if the component template supports it, nothing exceptional in principle, just a feature.

This is where it becomes problematic: it is possible, independently of the component template used, even if it is completely empty, to inject a slot containing an XSS payload, whose parent is a tag whose name is is the absolute path of the island file. Enabling reflected XSS on any application, regardless of the component templates used, provided that the server islands is used at least once.

### GitHub Vulnerability Alerts

#### [CVE-2025-64745](https://redirect.github.com/withastro/astro/security/advisories/GHSA-w2vj-39qv-7vh7)

## Summary

A Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability exists in Astro's development server error pages when the `trailingSlash` configuration option is used. An attacker can inject arbitrary JavaScript code that executes in the victim's browser context by crafting a malicious URL. While this vulnerability only affects the development server and not production builds, it could be exploited to compromise developer environments through social engineering or malicious links.

## Details

### Vulnerability Location

https://github.com/withastro/astro/blob/5bc37fd5cade62f753aef66efdf40f982379029a/packages/astro/src/template/4xx.ts#L133-L149

### Root Cause

The vulnerability was introduced in commit `536175528` (PR #​12994) , as part of a feature to "redirect trailing slashes on on-demand rendered pages." The feature added a helpful 404 error page in development mode to alert developers of trailing slash mismatches. [description truncated to fit budget]

#### [CVE-2025-62410](https://redirect.github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/security/advisories/GHSA-qpm2-6cq5-7pq5)

### Summary
The mitigation proposed in GHSA-37j7-fg3j-429f for disabling eval/Function when executing untrusted code in happy-dom does not suffice, since it still allows prototype pollution payloads.

### Details
The untrusted script and the rest of the application still run in the same Isolate/process, so attackers can deploy prototype pollution payloads to hijack important references like "process" in the example below, or to hijack control flow via flipping checks of undefined property. There might be other payloads that allow the manipulation of require, e.g., via (univeral) gadgets (https://www.usenix.org/system/files/usenixsecurity23-shcherbakov.pdf).

### PoC
Attackers can pollute builtins like Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty() to obtain important references at runtime, e.g., "process". In this way, attackers might be able to execute arbitrary commands like in the example below via spawn().

import { Browser } from "happy-dom";

const browser = new Browser({settings: {enableJavaScriptEvaluation: true}});
const page = browser.newPage({console: true}); [description truncated to fit budget]

### GitHub Vulnerability Alerts

#### [CVE-2025-61925](https://redirect.github.com/withastro/astro/security/advisories/GHSA-5ff5-9fcw-vg88)

### Summary
When running Astro in on-demand rendering mode using a adapter such as the node adapter it is possible to maliciously send an `X-Forwarded-Host` header that is reflected when using the recommended `Astro.url` property as there is no validation that the value is safe.

### Details
Astro reflects the value in `X-Forwarded-Host` in output when using `Astro.url` without any validation. 

It is common for web servers such as nginx to route requests via the `Host` header, and forward on other request headers. As such as malicious request can be sent with both a `Host` header and an `X-Forwarded-Host` header where the values do not match and the `X-Forwarded-Host` header is malicious. Astro will then return the malicious value.

This could result in any usages of the `Astro.url` value in code being manipulated by a request. For example if a user follows guidance and uses `Astro.url` for a canonical link the canonical link can be manipulated to another site. It is not impossible to imagine that the value could also be used as a login/registration or other form URL as well, resulting in potential redirecting of login credentials to a malicious party. This PR contains the following updates:

| Package | Type | Update | Change | OpenSSF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [happy-dom](https://redirect.github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom) | devDependencies | major | [`18.0.1` -> `20.0.0`](https://renovatebot.com/diffs/npm/happy-dom/18.0.1/20.0.0) | [![OpenSSF Scorecard](https://api.securityscorecards.dev/projects/github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/badge)](https://securityscorecards.dev/viewer/?uri=github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom) |

### GitHub Vulnerability Alerts

#### [CVE-2025-61927](https://redirect.github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/security/advisories/GHSA-37j7-fg3j-429f)

# Escape of VM Context gives access to process level functionality

## Summary
Happy DOM v19 and lower contains a security vulnerability that puts the owner system at the risk of RCE (Remote Code Execution) attacks.

A Node.js VM Context is not an isolated environment, and if the user runs untrusted JavaScript code within the Happy DOM VM Context, it may escape the VM and get access to process level functionality.

What the attacker can get control over depends on if the process is using ESM or CommonJS. With CommonJS the attacker can get hold of the `require()` function to import modules.

Happy DOM has JavaScript evaluation enabled by default. This may not be obvious to the consumer of Happy DOM and can potentially put the user at risk if untrusted code is executed within the environment.

## Reproduce

### CommonJS (Possible to get hold of require)

```javascript
const { Window } = require('happy-dom');
const window = new Window({ console });

window.document.write(`
  <script>
     const process = this.constructor.constructor('return process')();
     const require = process.mainModule.require;
  
     console.log('Files:', require('fs').readdirSync('.').slice(0,3));
  </script>
`);
```

### ESM (Not possible to get hold of import or require) [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: fix(graph): partition PR searches before fetching results
nodes.description:
The real bootstrap could not acquire its 12-month PR window: bulk pagination hit the subprocess timeout before the result-cap check could split the query.

Count results first, split oversized windows, then fetch one page per bounded request. This preserves the full window and older referenced PRs without increasing the 15-second timeout or 2 MB response limit.

## Changes
- Partition windows before fetching PR bodies and file metadata.
- Follow cursors explicitly and deduplicate overlapping boundaries.
- Reject stuck cursors, failed requests, count mismatches, and unsplittable over-cap windows instead of returning partial results.
- Update acquisition and fake-GitHub integration tests for the count/page response shapes.

## Verification
- `pnpm check`: passed.
- Scripts tests: 309 passed, none skipped.
- Live read-only acquisition: 1,114 unique PRs, matching an independent count for the same captured window; no duplicates or out-of-window results.
- 27 sequential requests completed in 60.3 seconds. The slowest request took 4.45 seconds; the largest response was 439,838 bytes. Limits were unchanged.

No graph build, acceptance, or promotion was performed.

nodes.title: test(docs): pin doctrine JSDoc parsing behavior
nodes.description:
Pins the JSDoc parsing behavior the documentation pipeline depends on, and brings `docs/` into the test graph for the first time.

## Why

`docs/scripts/extract-jsdoc.ts` parses every JSDoc comment that becomes API documentation, using `doctrine` — archived since 2018-12-03 (#2032).

Nothing is broken. The concern is how this pipeline fails. Two defects found recently produced silently wrong documentation while CI stayed green (#2017, #2022), and `docs/typedoc.json` sets `skipErrorChecking: true`, which turns resolution failures into bad output rather than errors (#2023).

`extract-jsdoc.ts:201` has the same shape:

```ts
} catch {
  // Continue looking for other comments
}
```

A parse failure is indistinguishable from "no JSDoc here."

## What it tests

Doctrine's `parse(text, {unwrap: true})` directly, with the exact options the pipeline uses, against fixtures taken from real components. The pipeline reads only two fields, so those are what get pinned:

```ts
description = jsdoc.description || ''
examples = jsdoc.tags?.filter(tag => tag.title === 'example')...
```

Seven tests: plain description, `@example` with an intact `tsx` code fence, multiple examples in source order, `@param`/`@returns`/`@remarks` not polluting the description, non-standard hyphenated tags, `@default`, and the short single-line prop comment form.

Fixtures 1-6 come from `Button.tsx` and `Form.tsx` verbatim or lightly condensed, cited in comments. Fixture 7 is synthetic — no verbatim single-line prop comments exist in the codebase today.

Assertions pin **observed** behavior, not ideal behavior. The point is detecting change.

## A finding, not a failure

Writing the test surfaced real silent corruption. Doctrine splits hyphenated tag names at the first hyphen:

```
@theme-tokens uses color.primary
  → tag title "theme",  description "-tokens uses color.primary" [description truncated to fit budget]

#2029 took `dompurify` from 3.1.7 to 3.4.8 by bumping `monaco-editor` to 0.56.0, which resolved 16 of the 20 open dompurify alerts. Four remain, each needing a later patch than monaco pins:

| Advisory | Severity | Vulnerable | Patched |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [GHSA-vxr8-fq34-vvx9](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vxr8-fq34-vvx9) | low | `< 3.4.9` | 3.4.9 |
| [GHSA-cmwh-pvxp-8882](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cmwh-pvxp-8882) | medium | `<= 3.4.10` | 3.4.11 |
| [GHSA-c2j3-45gr-mqc4](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c2j3-45gr-mqc4) | low | `<= 3.4.11` | 3.4.12 |
| [GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7) | medium | `<= 3.4.12` | 3.4.13 |

`dompurify` is transitive through `monaco-editor`, which pins it exactly at 3.4.8, so an override is the only lever until monaco ships a release pinning `>= 3.4.13`. Same shape as the three overrides in #2030.

Resolves to 3.4.14 after install. Reversible the moment monaco catches up.

## Remaining after this

Two alerts, both `image-size <= 2.0.2` ([GHSA-5p2g-fcmc-qvqq](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5p2g-fcmc-qvqq), [GHSA-w3rx-r6r6-pgpr](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-w3rx-r6r6-pgpr)), reached through `metro` ← `expo`. Neither has a patched release at any version, so there is nothing to override to. The pending Expo v57 bump does not help — a newer `metro` inherits the same unfixed dependency.

That takes the board from 31 open alerts to 2, both genuinely unfixable and both understood.

## Verification

- `pnpm test` 16/16 tasks
- `pnpm build` 10/10 tasks
- Post-install resolution: `dompurify@3.4.14`

nodes.title: chore(deps): remove abandoned @lhci/cli and its orphaned audit script
nodes.description:
Deletes a high-severity advisory rather than mitigating it.

`@lhci/cli` is flagged abandoned on the dependency dashboard — last release 2025-06-25 — and it drags in the only copy of `extract-zip <= 2.0.1`, [GHSA-jmr9-qjv8-65gv](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jmr9-qjv8-65gv). That advisory has **no patched release at any version**, so there is nothing to override to. The dependency was the advisory.

## Nothing invoked it

Its sole consumer was `scripts/accessibility-audit.sh`, and that script has no npm script, no workflow, and no reference anywhere outside the `.ai/` archive.

The script is 76 lines. Its only actual tool invocation:

```sh
npx lhci autorun --upload.target=filesystem --upload.outputDir=./lighthouse-reports \
  --collect.url="http://localhost:6006/iframe.html?id=form--default" \
  --collect.settings.chromeFlags="--no-sandbox" || true
```

Everything else is `echo` statements and a `curl` liveness check against Storybook. The `|| true` means even that one command swallowed its own failures.

It would not have worked regardless — `lighthouserc.js` is listed as FILE-009 in `.ai/plan/infrastructure-testing-framework-1.md` and was never written, so `lhci autorun` had no configuration to read.

## The audit that actually runs is unaffected

`docs/package.json` defines:

```json
"a11y:audit": "tsx scripts/accessibility-audit.ts",
"a11y:audit:ci": "tsx scripts/accessibility-audit.ts --ci"
```

That is a different file — `docs/scripts/accessibility-audit.ts` — and it imports only `node:fs`, `node:path`, and `node:process`. Lighthouse was never part of the path that runs.

Two accessibility-audit implementations existed with similar names; only the TypeScript one was ever wired up.

## Effect

`pnpm-lock.yaml` drops from 823134 to 784786 bytes — the whole `puppeteer-core` / `lighthouse` / `@puppeteer/browsers` subtree goes with it.

Open advisories go from 31 to 30, with one fewer high and no mitigation debt. [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: fix(deps): override three transitive packages with security advisories
nodes.description:
Clears 7 of the 31 open Dependabot alerts, including all four development-scope highs.

Every open alert is transitive through `pnpm-lock.yaml`, so an override is the only lever short of waiting for each intermediate package to bump on its own schedule.

## Changed

| Package | Installed | Override | Alerts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fast-uri` | 3.1.5 | ^3.1.6 (resolves 3.1.7) | **4 high** |
| `@xmldom/xmldom` | 0.8.14, 0.9.11 | ^0.8.15, ^0.9.12 | 2 medium |
| `decode-uri-component` | 0.2.2 | ^0.5.0 | 1 medium |

`fast-uri` reaches the tree through `ajv`, via `@microsoft/api-extractor` and `serve`. Worth noting for anyone re-checking: those advisories carry three separate version ranges each — 2.x, 3.x, and 4.x — and reading only the first suggests 3.1.5 is unaffected. It isn't; it falls inside `>= 3.1.3, < 3.1.6`.

`@xmldom/xmldom` has both its 0.8 and 0.9 lines installed, so both need pinning. A single `^0.8.15` would leave the 0.9 line vulnerable.

**20 alerts — dompurify.** All of them trace to `monaco-editor@0.54.0`, pinned exactly in `docs/package.json`. `monaco-editor@0.56.0` ships dompurify 3.4.8, and that bump is already sitting on the dependency dashboard as `renovate/monaco-editor-0.x`. Overriding dompurify here would paper over a real version bump that should happen properly — one checkbox does the same work with correct provenance.

**3 alerts — no patched release exists at any version.**

- `image-size` ≤ 2.0.2, 2 high, via `metro` ← `expo`
- `extract-zip` ≤ 2.0.1, 1 high, via `puppeteer-core` ← `lighthouse` ← `@lhci/cli`

Nothing to override to. The pending Expo v57 bump does not help — the advisory has no fixed version, so a newer `metro` inherits the same problem.

**1 alert — uuid.** Installed 7.0.3 and 8.3.2, both under `< 11.1.1`. Jumping four majors via override is not a change to make blind; it needs its own check of what depends on those lines.

nodes.title: docs: commit decision graph planning docs, revised for Deciduous v0.17.1
nodes.description:
First commit of three planning documents that have existed only in a working tree since May, plus a correction pass on the plan against the current version of its dependency.

## Why they were never committed

The plan doc carried a duplicate H1 — frontmatter `title:` plus a `# ` heading — which failed `markdown/no-multiple-h1`. That made `pnpm check` fail locally for anyone with these files present, so they stayed untracked. Fixed here; all three lint clean.

They were one `git clean -fd` from gone: an ideation record, a reviewed requirements doc, and a 730-line plan.

## Why the plan needed revising

It was written 2026-05-24 against Deciduous v0.15.0. Deciduous is now v0.17.1, and v0.17.0 replaced its persistence model entirely.

This plan's storage section has now been wrong twice, both times from reading source. So this pass ran the actual binary and revised against observed behavior.

### Storage model replaced

The committed surface is a Git-native record store — `.deciduous/sync/{nodes,edges,themes,tags}/*.json` — not the JSONL event logs and `checkpoint.json` the plan described. Generated `.gitignore`:

```gitignore
.deciduous/*
!.deciduous/config.toml
!.deciduous/sync/
```

`init` also writes a `.gitattributes` registering a custom merge driver (`.deciduous/sync/** merge=deciduous`), which the plan didn't know about and which changes the merge-conflict risk. SQLite is now a per-machine cache. `deciduous events rebuild` survives but is deprecated — a one-time legacy importer; `deciduous sync` is the rebuild path.

### The bootstrap cannot be re-run

This is the substantive change. Record files embed random UUIDs and wall-clock timestamps:

```json
{
  "change_id": "8e2fd008-d3e7-4c4a-b0b5-a93b3320fea8",
  "created_at": "2026-09-06T18:13:49.247436-07:00",
  "author": "Marcus R. Brown"
}
```

Two runs seeding identical content produced entirely disjoint record sets. Edge IDs derive from those UUIDs, so they churn too. [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: fix(docs): declare typedoc at the workspace root to unblock 0.28.20
nodes.description:
Unblocks the `typedoc` `0.28.19` → `0.28.20` upgrade that #1812 has been stuck on.

## The failure

```
[error] The plugin typedoc-plugin-frontmatter could not be loaded
[error] Cannot find package '<root>/node_modules/typedoc/index.js'
        imported from .../typedoc-plugin-frontmatter/dist/comments.js
        Did you mean to import "typedoc/dist/index.js"?
[error] Unknown option 'frontmatterGlobals'
```

CI-only. It never reproduced locally, under an identical lockfile, pnpm 11.25.0, and `shamefullyHoist: true`.

## What it actually was

`typedoc-plugin-frontmatter@1.3.1` imports `typedoc` with a bare specifier but declares no dependency on it — not in `dependencies`, not in `peerDependencies`, which list only `{"typedoc-plugin-markdown": ">=4.9.0"}`. pnpm therefore never links `typedoc` into the plugin's own `node_modules`, and resolution walks up to whatever hoisting leaves at the workspace root.

That is where the two environments diverged. Probing the runner directly:

```
node_modules/typedoc/          ← NOT a symlink
node_modules/typedoc/dist
node_modules/typedoc/dist/types    ← the entire contents
```

No `package.json`. Node cannot read an `exports` map that is not there, so it falls back to a legacy directory-index lookup and asks for `node_modules/typedoc/index.js`, which does not exist. Hence the error, and hence Node's "did you mean `typedoc/dist/index.js`?" hint — it never got as far as `exports`.

Locally the same hoist produces a complete symlink into `.pnpm`, `exports` resolves normally, and everything works. The plugin's own `node_modules` has sibling links for `typedoc-plugin-markdown` and `yaml`, but none for `typedoc`, on both platforms — the difference is entirely in what the root fallback happens to contain.

## The change [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: fix(ci): build packages before TypeDoc so cross-package types resolve
nodes.description:
CI has been generating API documentation without ever building the packages it documents, so every cross-package type reference silently resolved wrong.

`docs/src/content/docs/api/theme/src.md` documents:

```
> **mergeThemes**(`baseTheme`, `overrideTheme`): `ThemeConfig`
```

The source says otherwise — `packages/theme/src/utils/token-transformer.ts:276`:

```ts
mergeThemes(baseTheme: ThemeConfig, overrideTheme: Partial<ThemeConfig>): ThemeConfig
```

`Partial<ThemeConfig>`, not `ThemeConfig`. There is one `mergeThemes` in the package, so this is not a mis-documented overload.

## The mechanism

Three things line up:

1. `.github/actions/setup-ci` ends at `pnpm install`. It never builds.
2. Every `@sparkle/*` package resolves only through `dist` — `@sparkle/types` exports `{".": {"types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "import": "./dist/index.js"}}` — and `dist` is gitignored, so it does not exist on a fresh checkout.
3. `docs/typedoc.json` sets `skipErrorChecking: true`.

TypeDoc runs with `entryPointStrategy: resolve` against package **sources**, so `packages/theme/src` parses fine. But resolving `ThemeConfig`, which `@sparkle/theme` imports from `@sparkle/types`, goes through that `exports` map into a `dist` that is not there.

`skipErrorChecking` means that failure is not raised. TypeDoc mis-resolves the reference and keeps going, and `Partial<ThemeConfig>` renders as bare `ThemeConfig`. The docs are wrong and nothing is red.

Locally the same command is correct, because a local tree almost always has `dist` present from a previous build. That is why this survived: it only reproduces on a clean checkout, which is exactly what CI does every time and a developer almost never does.

## Isolated to one variable

Both runs invoke `typedoc --options typedoc.json` directly, not through the automation wrapper, so the pipeline is not part of the result: [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: chore(ci): require the Fro Bot check on main
nodes.description:
Makes `Fro Bot` a required status check on `main`.

```diff
-        contexts: [Build, Check, Renovate / Renovate, Setup]
+        contexts: [Build, Check, Fro Bot, Renovate / Renovate, Setup]
```

## Why now

It has been advisory since it landed. Over this session it caught eight substantive defects across consecutive PRs, including several I introduced and would otherwise have shipped:

- a `mode: maintenance` dispatch that would have resolved to `branch-pr`, contradicting the prompt's own instruction not to open PRs
- a code-point vs UTF-16 offset divergence in tab completion that corrupted any command line containing an emoji
- three missing regression tests covering behavior changes documented in a PR body but never asserted
- a missing changeset on a published package whose runtime behavior changed

Each was found by independently reproducing the work rather than reading the diff — running the affected suites, checking out the pre-PR file to confirm a failure was pre-existing, introspecting the resolved ESLint config. That is the level of review worth blocking on.

## Why a skipped run does not deadlock

This is the non-obvious part, and it is the reason the check was left advisory until now.

`Fro Bot` is conditional — it skips fork PRs, `[bot]`-authored PRs, and its own PRs via a job-level `if:` at `fro-bot.yaml:628`. GitHub documents that a job skipped by a job-level condition reports its status as **Success** and does not block a required check.

The case that *does* deadlock is workflow-level skipping — `paths`, `paths-ignore`, or `branches` filters, or `[skip ci]` — where no check run is ever posted and the requirement sits at `Expected` indefinitely.

`fro-bot.yaml`'s `on.pull_request` carries only `types:`, with no path or branch filters, so it always posts a check. Verified before making the change, along with the job `name:` matching the context string exactly. [description truncated to fit budget]

The docs-regeneration cache key never tracked package source.

```yaml
key: docs-regen-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('packages/*/src/**/*.{ts,tsx}', 'docs/scripts/**/*.ts', 'docs/typedoc.json') }}
```

`hashFiles` uses `@actions/glob`, which does not support brace expansion. Running the real package against this repo:

| Pattern | Files matched |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/*/src/**/*.{ts,tsx}` | **0** |
| explicit per-extension patterns | **45** |

So the key only ever reflected `docs/scripts/**` and `docs/typedoc.json`.

This is the same hazard #1798 fixed in this file's `on.push.paths` block. The comment that fix left behind is still there:

```yaml
# Note: GitHub Actions path filters do not support brace expansion
# (e.g. `*.{ts,tsx}`), so each extension is listed as its own pattern.
```

The path filters were corrected; the cache key three sections down was not.

## Observable effect

Three separate commits that each modified `packages/*/src/**/*.ts` produced an identical cache key:

| Run | Commit | Files under `packages/*/src/` | Key |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 34038835477 | `a3947ca0` | 1 | `docs-regen-Linux-75fd6cd1…` |
| 34039565992 | `0d2c7912` | 2 | `docs-regen-Linux-75fd6cd1…` |
| 34052091514 | `5d7d15fb` | 2 | `docs-regen-Linux-75fd6cd1…` |
| 34060270681 | `7a20340f` | 3 | `docs-regen-Linux-0f58363f…` |

The last differs only because that commit also touched `docs/scripts/*.ts`, which is matched by a brace-free pattern.

## Scope — what this does and does not explain

This fixes a real defect: the cache key is now correct, and package source changes will invalidate it.

It is **not** established that this alone unfreezes generated documentation. The evidence is incomplete in a way worth stating rather than papering over. [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: refactor(theme): convert ThemeValidator to module-scope functions
nodes.description:
`ThemeValidator` was a stateless namespace — one public `validate` method over roughly fifteen private helpers, plus a field holding constant defaults. The instance existed only to group functions.

The conversion is an inversion rather than a rewrite, because the function form already existed and was already the public API:

```ts
export function validateTheme(theme: ThemeConfig, options?: ValidationOptions): ValidationResult {
  const validator = new ThemeValidator()
  // ...
}
```

Both real consumers — `ThemeProvider.tsx:211` and `NativeThemeProvider.tsx:190` — call `validateTheme`. Nothing in production ever constructed the class. So the helpers move to module scope, `validateTheme` becomes the implementation, and the wrapper goes away.

## Removing the export

`ThemeValidator` was exported from the package barrel, which would normally be breaking. `@sparkle/theme` is at `0.0.0` and has never been published — `npm view @sparkle/theme` returns 404 — so there are no consumers to break.

Deleted outright rather than left as a deprecated adapter. #2013 removed one of those from `moo-dang` for being pure indirection, and adding a new one here would repeat the pattern this codebase just cleaned up.

`validateTheme` and `isValidTheme` are unchanged and still exported.

## Behavior

Identical. Options thread through to the helpers explicitly instead of via instance state; no validation rule, error message, or `ValidationResult` shape changed.

The test file is the safety net for that claim. It went from 49 assertions to 48 — the single removal being `expect(validator).toBeInstanceOf(ThemeValidator)`, which tested implementation rather than behavior. Every remaining assertion is unchanged; the only edits are mechanical `validator.validate(...)` → `validateTheme(...)` swaps.

## Also

Removes the `no-restricted-syntax` suppression added in #2015, which read: [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: docs: replace absolute class-avoidance rule with justified-exception rule + lint
nodes.description:
The class convention was an absolute ban that the codebase violated constantly:

> Avoid ES6 classes except for Error extensions

It appeared in four places with the same wording, and #1937 has been re-reporting violations against it on every nightly pass.

## Why the rule changed rather than the code

The rule is unambiguous but false. Enforcing it as written would mean converting a fluent builder whose entire API is method chaining, a transformer that owns cache lifecycle, and the shell subsystems that own process and job state — spending regression budget to make syntax uniform while leaving behavior identical.

Its actual intent is narrower: no classes as namespaces, no static utility bags, no passive data holders, no application inheritance hierarchies. Stateful objects with real lifecycle were never the target.

Seven classes flagged by the audit have already been deleted as genuinely unjustified — a dormant module in #2012 and a deprecated forwarding adapter in #2013. What remains earns its keep.

## New rule

> Prefer functions and closure factories. Classes are allowed only for `Error` or required platform subclasses, fluent builders, or cohesive stateful resources with meaningful instance lifecycle or identity. Do not use classes as namespaces, static utility bags, passive data holders, or application inheritance hierarchies. Every permitted standalone class must carry a local lint suppression explaining why a factory would be less clear.

Updated in `.github/copilot-instructions.md` (both the checklist entry and the detailed convention), `llms.txt`, and the `fro-bot.yaml` autoheal prompt. The quick-reference locations get a condensed form; `llms.txt` already points at `copilot-instructions.md` for the full set.

## Enforcement

Documentation-only has already failed once, so the rule is now mechanical: [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: fix(moo-dang): dispose JobControlSystem cleanup interval
nodes.description:
`JobControlSystem` started a 30-second cleanup interval in its constructor and discarded the handle:

```ts
private startCleanupTimer(): void {
  setInterval(() => {
    this.cleanup()
  }, 30000) // Run cleanup every 30 seconds
}
```

No `clearInterval` anywhere, and `JobController` had no disposal method — so the timer ran until its execution context died.

## Blast radius

Bounded in production. `ShellEnvironment`'s constructor creates the controller, `shell.worker.ts` creates one environment, and `App.tsx:97` calls `worker.terminate()`, which tears the interval down with the worker.

The real accumulation is in tests. `job-controller.test.ts` builds a controller per test, and every suite that constructs a `ShellEnvironment` builds another — each leaking an interval into the vitest process for the length of the run.

Proven rather than asserted: spying on `cleanup()` and advancing fake timers by 5 × 30s against an undisposed controller records exactly 5 invocations. After `dispose()`, the same advance records 0.

## Change

Stores the handle as `ReturnType<typeof setInterval>`, which covers both the DOM and Node timer types — relevant here because this runs inside a Web Worker.

Adds `dispose()` to `JobController` and implements it idempotently, clearing the stored handle so a second call is a no-op. `ShellEnvironment` owns the controller, so it gains a matching `dispose()` that delegates — naming follows `Terminal.tsx`, which already uses `dispose()`.

Tests now dispose in `afterEach`.

## Deliberately not done

**No worker teardown was added.** `shell.worker.ts` has no `close` handler, `self.onclose`, or shutdown message path. Inventing a worker lifecycle to call disposal would be scope creep for a leak that `terminate()` already handles — so production is untouched and the disposal contract exists for the owners that actually need it. [description truncated to fit budget]

chore(moo-dang): remove dormant performance-optimizations module
nodes.description:
`apps/moo-dang/src/utils/performance-optimizations.ts` has no consumers. 571 lines exporting `OptimizedCache`, `ArrayBufferPool`, `StringProcessor`, `LazyLoader`, `Debouncer`, `PerformanceMonitor`, two cache-value interfaces, a `globalOptimizations` singleton, and `initializeOptimizations` / `cleanupOptimizations` helpers — none of it reachable.

## Verification that it is dormant

- Every exported symbol searched by name repo-wide: only self-references inside the file. The one near-miss, `BuildPerformanceMonitor` in `docs/scripts/build-performance.ts`, is a different symbol in an unrelated file.
- Dynamic `import(` / `require(` searched across `apps/moo-dang`: 28 hits, none referencing this module.
- `apps/moo-dang/src/utils/index.ts` re-exports `accessibility-keyboard`, `output-formatting`, `scrollback-manager`, and `terminal-keys` only. The app's sole `export *` is in `src/components/index.ts`, a different directory.
- No config, build, or workflow references.
- No test file existed for it.

The only mention anywhere is `.ai/audit/audit-phase2-analysis.md`, an archived planning document.

## Why delete rather than keep

Beyond being unreachable, an architectural review flagged a likely defect in `OptimizedCache`'s eviction scoring around lines 97-102: increasing age raises an entry's score, but the ascending sort evicts the lowest score — so it appears to evict newer entries rather than older ones. Nobody can hit it, because nothing calls it.

That matters for the decision. This is not working code waiting for a consumer; it is unexercised code with at least one suspected bug in its core policy. Reviving it later should mean rewriting it against real requirements, not trusting six-hundred lines that have never run.

Keeping it also has a recurring cost. Six of the twelve classes flagged by the convention audit in #1937 live in this file, so every nightly pass re-reports them.

Git history retains it if it is ever wanted. [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: fix(moo-dang): use real shell tokenizer for tab completion
nodes.description:
Tab completion split the command line on whitespace, so a quoted argument containing a space was torn into separate tokens. Completing `cat "my doc<TAB>` saw `['cat', '"my', 'doc']` and matched candidates against `doc` instead of `my doc`.

```ts
// Parse command parts using simple whitespace splitting for now
// TODO: Enhance with proper shell parsing that handles quotes, escaping, etc.
const commandParts = inputToCursor.trim().split(/\s+/).filter(part => part.length > 0)
```

## The second instance

Fixing the tokenizer alone would not have been enough. `applySuggestion` independently re-derived the word boundary when a provider does not set an explicit `suggestion.range` — which is every provider today:

```ts
const words = beforeCursor.split(/\s+/)
const currentWord = words.at(-1) ?? ''
const wordStart = beforeCursor.lastIndexOf(currentWord)
```

Two problems. It repeats the same whitespace assumption, and `lastIndexOf` searches the entire prefix rather than locating the current token — so a repeated word matches the wrong occurrence. Accepting a completion on `cat "my doc` produced `cat "my my doc.txt`: quote stranded, wrong span replaced.

This is the path that actually corrupts the user's input, and it needed the span data, which is why the offset has to travel through `CompletionContext` rather than staying local to `createCompletionContext`.

## Approach

`parser.ts` already had a quote-aware state machine that tolerates unterminated quotes — `parseCommand('echo "unclosed')` returns `['echo', 'unclosed']` rather than throwing, which matters because mid-typing input almost always has an open quote. What it lacked was raw position: `parseCommand` returns stripped strings, and a stripped token cannot tell you where its opening quote was. [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: fix(moo-dang): remove non-functional performance regression check
refactor(types): replace actionable any usages with precise types
nodes.description:
Replaces the `any` usages that had real types available, and leaves alone the ones that don't.

The repo has 24 `any` occurrences. Auditing them turned out to matter more than fixing them: 16 are load-bearing, and a blanket cleanup would have made three of them worse.

## Changed

### `(error as any).exitCode` — 4 sites in `apps/moo-dang/src/shell/commands.ts`

`createShellCommandError` attaches `command` and `exitCode` via `Object.defineProperty` but declared its return type as plain `Error`, so every consumer had to cast to reach the fields it had just set.

Adds an exported `ShellCommandError` interface and an `isShellCommandError` guard, and narrows both factory return types. Consumers go from:

```ts
if (error instanceof Error && 'exitCode' in error && typeof (error as any).exitCode === 'number') {
  return createCommandResult(context, `...`, '', error.message, (error as any).exitCode, startTime)
}
```

to:

```ts
if (isShellCommandError(error)) {
  return createCommandResult(context, `...`, '', error.message, error.exitCode, startTime)
}
```

One assertion remains, at each factory's `return` — that is the single place the shape is actually constructed, and `Object.defineProperty` is invisible to the type system.

### `configManager.reset(options.section as any)`

`options.section` is a `string` straight from user input; `reset` takes a union of section literals. The cast was papering over a missing validation step, so an unknown section reached the config manager instead of producing an error.

Now validated through a type guard, returning a proper command error that matches the existing `config list: section '...' not found` style. This is the one intentional behavior change here — invalid input now fails cleanly rather than being asserted past.

The section list was previously a local array inside `_formatFullConfig`. It is now a module-level `CONFIG_SECTION_NAMES` shared by validation and display, declared as: [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: test(theme): hoist NullContextWrapper to module scope
nodes.description:
Unblocks #1956, the `@bfra.me/eslint-config` bump to `0.52.1`.

That release enables `unicorn/consistent-function-scoping`, which produces exactly one error across the repo:

```
77:5  error  Move function 'NullContextWrapper' to the outer scope  unicorn/consistent-function-scoping
✖ 1 problem (1 error, 0 warnings)
```

`NullContextWrapper` provides `value={null}` to exercise the null-context branch of `useTheme`'s guard. It references only the module-level `ThemeContext` import and its own `children` prop, so nothing tied it to the test that declared it.

## Why the other wrappers stay put

`packages/theme/test/theme-hooks.test.tsx` has four inner wrappers. Only this one is flagged, and that is correct — the other three each capture a context value constructed inside their own test:

| Wrapper | Captures | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NullContextWrapper` | nothing | hoisted |
| `CustomWrapper` | `contextValueWithMockSetTheme` | unchanged |
| `LoadingWrapper` | `loadingContextValue` | unchanged |
| `ErrorWrapper` | `errorContextValue` | unchanged |

Hoisting any of the other three would require lifting their context values to module scope too, which would leak per-test state across tests. The rule is right to leave them alone.

## Verification

Checked against the real `0.52.1` config in an isolated worktree, since the rule does not exist in the version currently on `main`:

- **Control** — original file reproduces the CI error exactly: `77:5 ... 1 problem (1 error, 0 warnings)`
- **After** — `npx eslint .` across the whole repo exits `0`
- `pnpm --filter @sparkle/theme test` — 8 files, 164 tests passing

The control run matters here: an earlier attempt to force the rule on without the plugin installed produced a misleading exit `0` because the rule never actually ran.

nodes.title: docs(llms): stop duplicating the pinned pnpm version
nodes.description:
`llms.txt` restates the pinned pnpm version, which means it goes stale on every Renovate bump.

This is the third time it has drifted:

- Original value: `pnpm@10.33.4`
- #1816 corrected it to `pnpm@11.17.0`
- Repo is already on `pnpm@11.25.0`

Each fix restores accuracy and resets the clock. Issue #1800 has been reopened by the same drift twice now.

## Change

```diff
-- Package manager: **pnpm** (root `packageManager: pnpm@11.17.0`)
+- Package manager: **pnpm** — exact version pinned by `packageManager` in the root `package.json`
```

Point at the source of truth instead of copying the value out of it. Nothing left to drift.

## Why not just bump it

Bumping restores the value but guarantees a fourth occurrence. The autoheal report has flagged this line repeatedly; the recurring cost is the report noise and the review cycle, not the wrong digit.

## Why the Node line is untouched

```
- Node: pinned via `.node-version` (24.x) — repo `engines` floor is `>=22.13.1`
```

Different risk profile. It references `.node-version` loosely as `24.x` rather than pinning an exact patch, and quotes the `engines` floor verbatim — both currently accurate (`.node-version` is `24.20.0`, `engines.node` is `>=22.13.1`). It degrades gracefully across patch bumps instead of going stale on each one, so there is nothing to fix.

## Verification

- Only remaining version-like string in `llms.txt` is the Node line above, confirmed accurate against `.node-version` and `package.json`
- No other file references the removed value

Closes #1800

nodes.title: fix(ci): request branch-pr delivery for Fro Bot autoheal runs
nodes.description:
Follow-up to #2001. That PR restored a pushable git remote, but autoheal fixes still had nowhere to land — the credential was never the binding constraint.

## The actual rule

`fro-bot/agent` resolves delivery mode from one action input:

```ts
resolveOutputMode(eventType, configuredMode)
```

For `schedule` and `workflow_dispatch`:

| configured | resolved |
| --- | --- |
| `working-dir` | `working-dir` |
| `branch-pr` | `branch-pr` |
| `auto` (default) | **`working-dir`** |

Every other event type returns `null` and ignores the input entirely.

The resolver takes no credential, actor, or filesystem input. An on-disk `extraheader` has no bearing on the result. `action.yaml` states it directly:

> Manual auto requests always resolve to working-dir; use branch-pr explicitly when branch/PR delivery is required.

Source: [`packages/runtime/src/agent/output-mode.ts`](https://github.com/fro-bot/agent/blob/main/packages/runtime/src/agent/output-mode.ts)

## Why this was missed

This workflow never set `output-mode`, so it fell through to the `auto` compatibility default and resolved to `working-dir` on every run — schedule and dispatch alike.

The daily autohealing report (#1665) attributed the failure to a missing credential step, citing `marcusrbrown/mrbro.dev` as having the fix. That difference was real, and #2001 ported it. But `mrbro.dev` does not set `output-mode` either, so it resolves to `working-dir` too. The comparison found a genuine difference between the repos and attributed causation to it without establishing that it was the operative one.

#2001 remains a prerequisite — once `branch-pr` is active the agent needs a credential to actually push — but it was not sufficient on its own.

## Change

Requests `branch-pr` explicitly for the paths that need to deliver fixes: [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: fix(deps): consolidate outstanding security overrides
nodes.description:
Closes three high-severity advisories that each had their own bot-authored PR.

## Why one PR instead of three rebases

`#1838`, `#1866`, and `#1862` all edit the same `overrides` block in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. Once the nanoid override landed in `#1904`, the remaining three conflicted against `main` and against each other — same two files, same conflict class every time. Rebasing them sequentially means three rounds of the same merge resolution. One entry point is cheaper and easier to review.

## Overrides added

| Package | Floor | Advisory | Resolves to | Replaces |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `adm-zip` | `^0.6.0` | GHSA-xcpc-8h2w-3j85 | 0.6.0 | #1838 |
| `brace-expansion` | `^5.0.8` | GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg | 5.0.9 | #1866 |
| `postcss` | `^8.5.23` | GHSA-r28c-9q8g-f849 | 8.5.26 | #1862 |

## Note on the postcss floor

`#1862`'s title says `^8.5.12`, but its actual diff already targeted `^8.5.18` — the title was stale. `^8.5.18` clears the high advisory (GHSA-r28c-9q8g-f849) but leaves medium GHSA-fxqj-rqcc-2cmp open. This raises the floor to `^8.5.23` so both are closed by constraint rather than by whatever resolution happens to land.

## Verification

- `pnpm install` resolves cleanly; lockfile shrinks 819723 → 818697 bytes
- Resolved versions confirmed against the lockfile: `adm-zip 0.6.0`, `brace-expansion 5.0.9`, `postcss 8.5.26`, `nanoid 3.3.18`
- `pnpm check` — exit 0
- `pnpm build` — 10/10 tasks, docs site builds 71 pages

## Follow-up

Supersedes #1838, #1866, #1862 — those should close once this merges.

Advisories the autohealing report flagged as unremediable are unaffected and remain open: `fast-uri` (transitive via `ajv`, dev-only), `extract-zip` (no patched version upstream), `image-size` (no patched version, Expo/Metro toolchain).

nodes.title: fix(ci): enable authenticated git push for Fro Bot autoheal runs
nodes.description:
Scheduled autoheal runs have had no pushable git remote, so every fix the agent produced degraded to `working-dir` mode and had nowhere to land. The daily autohealing report (#1665) has flagged this "fixes never persist" pattern for weeks.

## Root cause

The checkout step uses `persist-credentials: false` to keep the PAT out of `.git/config` on the fork-PR-head comment path. Nothing restores a credential afterward for the paths that legitimately need to push, so `fro-bot/agent` runs with an unauthenticated remote.

`marcusrbrown/mrbro.dev` already solves this; sparkle never got the equivalent step.

## Change

Writes the PAT to `http.https://github.com/.extraheader` after checkout, masked via `::add-mask::`.

Gated to the 05:00 autoheal cron and dispatched autoheal runs only:

```yaml
if: >-
  (github.event_name == 'schedule' && github.event.schedule == '0 5 * * *')
  || (github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.mode == 'autoheal')
```

This is tighter than the mrbro.dev original, which gates on `github.event_name == 'schedule'` generally. Sparkle runs autoheal and maintenance on separate crons, and `MAINTENANCE_PROMPT` forbids opening PRs — it only updates one perpetual issue, which the API token already covers. So the 17:00 maintenance cron is excluded. Review-mode dispatch is excluded for the same reason.

Mention and `issue_comment` runs are deliberately excluded: the agent classifies those as credential-withheld and fails closed if it finds an on-disk `http.*.extraheader`, so writing one there would break the agent rather than enable push.

The credential goes to disk rather than env or the gh credential helper because the agent scrubs its child environment.

## Verification

- `actionlint .github/workflows/fro-bot.yaml` — exit 0
- YAML parses; the step lands between `Setup project` and `Run Fro Bot`
- 32 additive lines, one file, no existing lines modified

## Known edge [description truncated to fit budget]

Daily autohealing convention-compliance scan found three docs source files still using `console.*` instead of `consola`, not covered by any existing open PR (#1886 and #1891 covered other files in this same cleanup effort).

nodes.title: fix(deps): override nanoid to ^3.3.17 to remediate GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8
nodes.description:
## Summary

Remediates a **high severity** Dependabot alert (#227, [GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8](https://github.com/marcusrbrown/sparkle/security/dependabot/227)): `nanoid` versions `<3.3.17` allow custom generators to loop indefinitely when `size` is zero.

`nanoid` is a transitive dependency pulled in via `@react-navigation/core` (through `expo-router` in `apps/fro-jive`). No direct usage in Sparkle source.

## Changes

- Added a pnpm override in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`: `nanoid@<3.3.17: ^3.3.17`
- Regenerated `pnpm-lock.yaml`; `nanoid` now resolves to `3.3.17` (patched) everywhere in the tree

## Verification

- `pnpm check` — clean (0 errors, pre-existing markdown warnings only)
- `pnpm check:monorepo` (manypkg) — valid
- `pnpm build` — all 10 Turborepo tasks succeed

nodes.title: fix(moo-dang): add missing @sparkle/test-utils workspace dependency
nodes.description:
## What
Adds `@sparkle/test-utils` as a `workspace:*` devDependency of `apps/moo-dang`.

## Why
`pnpm test` on `main` was failing: 6 of 17 moo-dang test files (`App.test.tsx`, `shell-e2e.test.tsx`, `help-command-fix.test.tsx`, `components/Terminal.test.tsx`, `shell/wasm.test.ts`, `shell/wasm-integration.test.ts`) import from `@sparkle/test-utils` subpaths (`/console`, `/dom`, `/react`, `/terminal`), but the package was never declared as a dependency in `apps/moo-dang/package.json`. Under pnpm's strict, non-hoisted linking this left the package unresolved in `node_modules`, breaking Vite's module resolution for every test file that imports it.

## Fix
- Added `"@sparkle/test-utils": "workspace:*"` to `devDependencies` (matches internal-dependency convention).
- Regenerated `pnpm-lock.yaml`.

## Verification
- `pnpm check` — clean (manypkg, types, turbo config, dependency validation, lint)
- `pnpm build` — 10/10 Turborepo tasks green
- `pnpm test` — 17/17 test files, 445 passed / 1 skipped (previously 11/17 files, 358 passed)
- `pnpm fix` — no additional diff

---

nodes.title: fix(docs): remove broken system-ui.woff2 font preload
nodes.description:
## What

Removes a site-wide `<link rel="preload">` for `/fonts/system-ui.woff2` from `docs/astro.config.mjs`.

## Why

`system-ui` is the native OS font-family keyword (already used in `docs/src/styles/sparkle-theme.css` — `--sparkle-font-family-sans: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", ...`), not a downloadable web font. No file was ever added under `docs/public/fonts/`, so this preload has 404'd on every single page load since it was introduced in #911 (2025-09-11).

Found during the daily autohealing live docs-site-health check (`https://sparkle.mrbro.dev`) via `agent-browser network requests`:

```
GET https://sparkle.mrbro.dev/fonts/system-ui.woff2 (Font) 404
```

Reported as a minor finding in the last two daily autohealing updates without a fix; since the root cause and fix are unambiguous and minimal (delete an 11-line dead config block), fixing directly here.

## Verification

- `pnpm --filter @sparkle/docs build` — succeeds, 71 pages built, `dist/` no longer references `system-ui.woff2`
- `pnpm check` — clean
- `pnpm fix` — no additional changes needed

nodes.title: fix(theme): correct spacing scale consistency check for zero-anchored scales
nodes.description:
## What
Fixes a bug in `ThemeValidator`'s spacing scale consistency check (`packages/theme/src/validators/theme-validator.ts`) discovered via `pnpm test` failing on `main` during daily autohealing.

## Root cause
The geometric-progression check used a truthy guard (`prevValue && currentValue && nextValue`) to decide whether to compute a ratio window. Since `0` is a common/valid spacing baseline, any window anchored on a `0` value was silently skipped — not because of the intended division-by-zero concern, but as a side effect of JS truthiness. Combined with a loose `0.5` tolerance, this meant `theme-validator.test.ts > should treat warnings as errors in strict mode` never received the expected warning for an intentionally inconsistent scale (`0px, 4px, 10px, 20px`).

## Fix
- Replace the truthy guard with explicit `undefined`/`0` checks, so zero-anchored windows are skipped for the right reason (avoiding `x / 0`) rather than by accident.
- Tighten the ratio tolerance from `0.5` to `0.3` so a `2.5x` → `2x` jump is correctly flagged as inconsistent, matching the test's intent.

## Verification
- `pnpm --filter @sparkle/theme test` — 164/164 passing (was 163/164)
- `pnpm test` — full workspace suite green
- `pnpm check` — clean (format + types + monorepo consistency)
- `pnpm build` — clean

---
🤖 Filed by the [Fro Bot daily autohealing run](https://github.com/marcusrbrown/sparkle/issues/1665) (category 4/5: quality gate fix).

### [`v0.93.1`](https://redirect.github.com/fro-bot/agent/releases/tag/v0.93.1)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/fro-bot/agent/compare/v0.93.0...v0.93.1)

#### What's new

<!-- fro-bot-narration-v1 -->

The two fixes in this release address issues uncovered by the first live narration run (v0.93.0).

##### Bug fixes

The v0.93.0 candidate was rejected by the apply job because the narrative legitimately described the validator itself, using an inline code span containing `` `<details>` ``. The structural regex that guards against idempotency-marker or `<details>` forgery matched the code-quoted tag even though GitHub renders it as inert literal text. A new `stripCodeSpans()` helper blanks the contents of well-formed fenced code blocks and inline code spans before the `contains-marker` and `contains-details` checks run, leaving all other validation (empty body, oversized candidate, control characters, missing PR link) on the raw text. The fail-closed posture is preserved: an unbalanced backtick or unterminated fence leaves the raw text intact so a real tag hidden behind broken markup is still caught. nodes.title: fix(ci): use explicit path patterns in regenerate-docs path filter
nodes.description:
## What

`regenerate-docs.yaml`'s `push.paths` filter used brace-expanded
extension groups (e.g. `packages/ui/src/**/*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}`).
GitHub Actions path filters only support `*`/`**` glob wildcards —
brace expansion is not part of the supported filter syntax. This
workflow has **0 recorded runs** in its entire history, despite
numerous qualifying commits to `packages/{ui,types,utils,theme,error-testing}/src/**`.

## Fix

Expand each brace group into its own explicit path entry so the
trigger condition actually matches source file changes.

Also regenerated the one drifted API doc this silent failure caused:
`packages/theme/src/utils/token-transformer.ts`'s `mergeThemes`
already takes `Partial<ThemeConfig>` for its second parameter, but the
last-generated docs still showed the pre-change `ThemeConfig` type
(from #824).

## Verification

- `python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(...)"` — YAML parses cleanly
- `pnpm --filter @sparkle/docs docs:automation` — regenerates
  `docs/src/content/docs/api/theme/src.md` with no further diff
- `pnpm check` / `pnpm build` / `pnpm test` — clean on this branch

## Scope

Config-only change to a workflow trigger condition + one regenerated
doc file. No behavior changes to the documentation generation logic
itself.

nodes.title: fix(fro-bot): honor a bare workflow_dispatch prompt regardless of mode
nodes.description:
## What

A `workflow_dispatch` that passes only a custom `prompt` (no `mode`) had its prompt silently discarded. The `Run Fro Bot` step only consumed `inputs.prompt` when `inputs.mode == 'review'`, and `mode` defaults to `autoheal` — so a bare-prompt dispatch fell through to the autoheal prompt and ran the wrong task.

This surfaced when a cross-repo goal dispatch (which sends only the universal `prompt` input, since not every repo declares a `mode`) triggered an autoheal run here instead of the requested task.

## Fix

Let a non-empty `inputs.prompt` win first for any `workflow_dispatch`, before the mode-based selection:

```diff
-  (github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.mode == 'review' && inputs.prompt)
+  (github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.prompt)
```

This matches how the sibling repos wire prompt selection (`inputs.prompt` first, mode/schedule prompts as fallbacks). Behavior when no prompt is supplied is unchanged: maintenance/autoheal still fire by mode, and the separate review-mode input validation step is untouched.

## Verification

nodes.title: chore(lint): apply auto-fixes from autohealing run
nodes.description:
## What

Adds the missing `build:<package>` script alias to 8 workspace packages (`types`, `utils`, `error-testing`, `config`, `ui`, `storybook`, `docs`, `moo-dang`), matching the convention already used by `@sparkle/theme` (`"build:theme": "npm run build"`).

## Why

`turbo.json` defines package-qualified task dependencies such as `@sparkle/ui#build:ui` and `@sparkle/config#build:config` for the `test`, `dev`, `docs:automation`, and `build:docs` tasks. Turborepo silently no-ops a dependency edge when the target package has no script matching the task name — it does not error. Only `@sparkle/theme` had defined its `build:theme` alias; every other package listed above only had a generic `build` script, so those dependency edges never actually built anything.

**Concrete symptom**: on a clean checkout (no prior `pnpm build`), `pnpm test`'s `^build:ui` dependency never ran `packages/ui`'s `build:css` step, so `packages/ui/dist/styles.css` was missing. `moo-dang`'s component tests then failed with:

```
Error: Failed to resolve import "./styles.css" from "../../packages/ui/dist/index.js"
```

This wasn't caught by CI because `.github/workflows/main.yaml` only runs `pnpm check` and `pnpm build` — it doesn't run `pnpm test`.

## Fix

Add a `build:<package>` alias (`"npm run build"` / `"pnpm build"`) to each affected package, so the turbo task graph resolves as intended without depending on residual build output from an earlier full `pnpm build`.

## Verification

- Removed all `dist/` and `.turbo/` output across the workspace
- `pnpm test` → 445 passed, 1 skipped (17/17 files), `packages/ui/dist/styles.css` correctly generated via the dependency chain
- `pnpm check` → clean (manypkg, types, turbo config, dependency validation, lint all pass)
- `pnpm build` → all 10 tasks successful
- `pnpm check:monorepo` → workspaces valid

---
🤖 Opened by the [Fro Bot daily autohealing run](https://github.com/marcusrbrown/sparkle/issues/1665).

nodes.title: fix(turbo): add @sparkle/test-utils#build dependency to test tasks
nodes.description:
## Problem

On a cold Turborepo cache, `moo-dang` tests fail with:

```
Error: Failed to resolve import "@sparkle/test-utils/dom" from "src/components/Terminal.test.tsx"
Error: Failed to resolve import "@sparkle/test-utils/console" from "src/shell/wasm-integration.test.ts"
```

The `moo-dang` test suite imports from `@sparkle/test-utils` subpath exports (`/dom`, `/console`, `/terminal`) which require the `dist/` directory to be populated. However, the `test` Turbo task only depended on `build:utils`, `build:theme`, `build:config`, and `build:ui` — not on `@sparkle/test-utils#build`.

`@sparkle/test-utils` uses the generic `build` task (not a named `build:test-utils`), so it was not included in the test dependency chain. On a warm cache this is masked; on a cold cache the 6 affected test files fail.

## Fix

Add `@sparkle/test-utils#build` as an explicit dependency in the `test`, `test:coverage`, and `test:watch` Turbo tasks.

## Verification

- `pnpm test` passes: 445 tests, 1 skipped ✅
- `pnpm build` clean: 10/10 tasks ✅

nodes.title: fix(security): bump tmp override to ^0.2.6 to address CVE-2026-44705
nodes.description:
## Summary

Remediates **CVE-2026-44705** / **GHSA-ph9p-34f9-6g65** (high severity): path traversal via unsanitized `prefix`/`postfix` in the `tmp` package, allowing directory escape.

## What changed

Updated `pnpm-workspace.yaml` override:
```diff
-  tmp@<0.2.4: ^0.2.4
+  tmp@<0.2.6: ^0.2.6
```

The previous override resolved to `tmp@0.2.5` which is still vulnerable. The new override resolves to `tmp@0.2.7` (patched version: `0.2.6+`).

## Dependency chain

`tmp` is a transitive dependency (devDependency only) via:
- `@lhci/cli@0.15.1` → `inquirer@6.5.2` → `external-editor@3.1.0` → `tmp`
- `@axe-core/cli@4.11.3` → `selenium-webdriver` → `tmp`

## Verification

- `pnpm why tmp` confirms `tmp@0.2.7` is now installed
- All 445 tests pass (after build)
- Build pipeline clean

nodes.title: feat(ci): add Fro Bot workflow + llms.txt project map
nodes.description:
Brings sparkle to agent-native parity with marcusrbrown/marcusrbrown and mrbro.dev. After 6 months of pure Renovate-only automation, this wires the unified Fro Bot template into sparkle.

## What

### `.github/workflows/fro-bot.yaml` (new, 740 lines)

Unified workflow — one file handles three modes:

| Mode | Triggers | Cadence |
|---|---|---|
| **Review** | PR open/sync/reopen/ready_for_review/review_requested, `@fro-bot` mention in comments | On-event |
| **Maintenance** | `schedule`, `workflow_dispatch` | 17:00 UTC daily |
| **Autoheal** | `schedule`, `workflow_dispatch` | 05:00 UTC daily |

Schedule slots staggered off siblings: marcusrbrown (04:30/16:30), mrbro.dev (03:30/15:30).

**Guards copied from upstream template:**
- Bot author + fork PR skip at the job-level `if:`
- `OWNER/MEMBER/COLLABORATOR` author-association required for comment triggers
- Fork-PR-head refusal on `issue_comment`-triggered checkouts (the comment payload lacks the fork flag the job-level guard relies on)
- Concurrency keyed on issue/PR/discussion number with `cancel-in-progress: false`
- Sunday UTC detection feeds `IS_SUNDAY_UTC` for category 8 cadence

### Sparkle-tailored prompts [description truncated to fit budget]

nodes.title: chore: clean the board
nodes.description:
Restores signal on the repo root before the next round of feature work.

## What

- Drop `docs-legacy/` (60KB, deprecated since Sep 2025; explicitly redirected callers to the live docs site and all content has been migrated)
- Refresh `readme.md`:
  - Add missing `apps/moo-dang` (WASM web shell) and `@sparkle/test-utils` packages
  - Correct prerequisites (pnpm >=10, the repo pins `packageManager: pnpm@10.33.4`)
  - Fix stale `./docs/project-guide.md` and `./docs/best-practices-for-sparkle-development.md` references (those files were inside `docs-legacy/`)
  - Update the architecture tree to reflect the actual `apps/` vs `packages/` split and the live package set
  - Point Resources to <https://sparkle.mrbro.dev> and the existing `.github/copilot-instructions.md`

## Why

The README and the deprecated `docs-legacy/` directory had drifted ~7 months out of date. The audit, the docs migration, and the moo-dang/test-utils packages all landed without README updates. New contributors and agents land on a README that misses half the surface area.

## Verification

- `pnpm check` clean
- No live code or workflow files reference `docs-legacy/` (only `.specstory/history/` historic Cursor logs)
- Live docs site is the canonical surface

## Related

- Closes #57 (Uplift sparkle — all three checklist items effectively complete)
- Diagnosis posted on #1604 (Astro 6 + Starlight 0.36 incompatibility; needs grouped Starlight >=0.39 upgrade)

### GitHub Vulnerability Alerts

#### [CVE-2026-33943](https://redirect.github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/security/advisories/GHSA-6q6h-j7hj-3r64)

### Summary

A code injection vulnerability in `ECMAScriptModuleCompiler` allows an attacker to achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE) by injecting arbitrary JavaScript expressions inside `export { }` declarations in ES module scripts processed by happy-dom. The compiler directly interpolates unsanitized content into generated code as an executable expression, and the quote filter does not strip backticks, allowing template literal-based payloads to bypass sanitization.

### Details

**Vulnerable file**: `packages/happy-dom/src/module/ECMAScriptModuleCompiler.ts`, lines 371-385

The "Export object" handler extracts content from `export { ... }` using the regex `export\s*{([^}]+)}`, then generates executable code by directly interpolating it: [description truncated to fit budget]
